slides.title: Place and limits of the method
bullets: Counting red cells gives general quantitative information and is done when anaemia is suspected.
Cells are counted under the microscope in a set number of squares of the grid; from the volume of the squares and the dilution the result is converted to 1 µL of blood.
The Aripova book notes that the counting-chamber method is not very accurate and is usually not recommended: modern laboratories are being equipped with rapid automated analysers.
Many laboratories nevertheless use the Goryaev chamber; to reduce errors the large squares of the grid are counted.

slides.title: Materials and reagents
bullets: Diluent: a formol-citrate solution in the Aripova book, 0.9% sodium chloride in the QVP book; in both, 20 µL of blood is added to 4 mL of diluent (1:200).
A counting chamber and its matching cover glass; a pipette or glass rod to fill the chamber.
Stoppered tubes, a 20 µL (0.02 mL) pipette, a rubber bulb.

slides.title: Materials and reagents
bullets: A microscope (10× and 40× objectives, 10× eyepiece). The chamber and cover glass are washed with water and wiped dry beforehand.

slides.title: Dilution and filling the chamber
bullets: 1. Pour 4 mL of diluent into each tube and label it with the number from the patient’s requisition.
2. Fill the pipette with blood to 20 µL; check for bubbles and that the blood is at the mark; wipe the pipette outside.

3. Expel the blood to the bottom of the tube with a rubber bulb or an automatic pipette (never by mouth), rinse the pipette in the upper layer of the liquid; mix the contents thoroughly (Aripova: 2 minutes).

slides.title: Dilution and filling the chamber
bullets: 4. Rub the cover glass onto the chamber until rainbow Newton’s rings appear.
5. Fill by touching the edge of the chamber with the pipette held at a small angle — do not overfill, avoid bubbles.
6. Leave the chamber to let the cells settle (Aripova: 2 minutes; QVP: 1 minute), then put it on a horizontal stage.

slides.title: Counting and calculation
bullets: First focus on the centre of the chamber with the 10× objective, then on the grid with the 40× objective and weak light.
In the Goryaev chamber count the red cells in 5 large squares (80 small ones) along a diagonal.
Count the cells inside the square and those touching its upper and left lines; do not count those on the right and lower lines (they belong to the next square).
Formula: X = a × 4000 × dilution / number of small squares counted (a small square holds 1/4000 µL).

slides.title: Counting and calculation
bullets: With 80 small squares and a 1:200 dilution it is enough to multiply the count by 10 000: 400 cells → 4.0 × 10^12/L.
Ranges in the books: men 4.5–6.5, women 4.4–6.0 × 10^12/L.

slides.title: Sources of error
bullets: Clots of blood: they trap some of the cells and lower the result.
Insufficient mixing of the tube contents before filling the chamber; uneven distribution of cells in the chamber is a frequent source of error.
The cover glass is badly seated, without rings — the chamber volume changes.
Counting right after filling, without waiting for the cells to settle — the result is lower than the true value.
Too few squares counted, or poorly washed capillaries.
Counting is advised within 2–3 hours of sampling; in haemolytic and megaloblastic anaemia, immediately.

slides.title: Quality control
bullets: For the counting-chamber method there is little control against which to compare results, so every step of standardisation (mixing, seating the cover glass, settling time, counting rule) is carried out carefully.
Stabilised blood, special suspensions for checking cell counts, haemolysates and fixed smears are used as control materials.

slides.title: Safety
bullets: Treat all specimens as potentially infectious; blood work is done in rubber gloves with a single-use scarifier.
Never draw material into a pipette by mouth; use a rubber bulb.
Do not use glassware with chipped edges.

slides.title: Red blood cell count (RBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 1/2
bullets: Specimen: Venous blood (EDTA, purple-top tube)  ·  Units: ×10¹²/L, ×10⁶/µL
What it is used for: An RBC count is almost always part of a complete blood count and helps diagnose red blood cell disorders such as anemia.

An RBC count that is higher or lower than normal is often the first sign of an illness and may allow treatment before symptoms appear. The test is used during treatment that can affect blood counts (such as chemotherapy), to monitor conditions such as chronic kidney disease, and for symptoms of a low count (shortness of breath, weakness, headache, dizziness, arrhythmia, pale skin) or a high count (headache, dizziness, vision problems).

slides.title: Red blood cell count (RBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · What it is used for · 2/2
bullets: Physiology: Red blood cells are made in the bone marrow, the spongy tissue inside large bones. They contain hemoglobin, an iron-rich protein that carries oxygen from the lungs to every cell.

slides.title: Red blood cell count (RBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Interpreting the result
cols: Causes of a high RBC count include dehydration, heart disease, polycythemia vera, scarring of the lungs (often from smoking), lung disease, kidney cancer and sleep apnea. Misuse of performance drugs such as anabolic steroids and living at a high altitude can also raise it.

Causes of a low RBC count include anemia, leukemia, malnutrition (not enough calories, vitamins and/or minerals), multiple myeloma, kidney failure, blood loss from injury or other problems, alcohol use disorder and pregnancy.

slides.title: Red blood cell count (RBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 1/3
bullets: Pre-analytics: No special preparation is needed for this test.

Per the WHO phlebotomy guidelines, hematology tests use an EDTA tube (usually purple top): EDTA removes calcium by forming calcium salts. The tube needs a full draw and gentle inversion so the blood mixes thoroughly with the additive — poor mixing can give erroneous results. Cap colors may differ by manufacturer.

Interferences: Diet, activity level, medicines, having a menstrual period, not drinking enough water and other factors can affect CBC results; an abnormal level does not always mean a condition that needs treatment.

slides.title: Red blood cell count (RBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 2/3
bullets: Analyser errors: RBC can be falsely high with marked leukocytosis or hyperlipidaemia and falsely low with cold agglutinins or in-tube haemolysis. In cold agglutination red cells are counted as clumps — RBC is low while MCV and MCHC are falsely high. Dolgov et al. advise warming such a sample to 37 °C and re-measuring. If the result does not fit the clinical picture — flags, smear and repeat.
Limitations: A complete blood count is only one tool: for a diagnosis the provider considers medical history, symptoms and other factors, and more tests may be needed.

slides.title: Red blood cell count (RBC)
slides.eyebrow: Hematology (complete blood count) · Pre-analytics and interferences · 3/3
bullets: If the count is low or high, more tests may be needed: a reticulocyte count (checks whether the bone marrow makes enough red cells), iron tests and B vitamin tests.
NHLBI notes that some normal ranges differ between men and women, and that age, high altitude and race may also affect them — so the result is compared with the range on the lab report.

slides.title: Example: Counting chamber
bullets: Formula: Cells/µL = cells counted × dilution ÷ (squares counted × area of one square, mm² × chamber depth, mm)
slides.ex: 1 µL = 1 mm³; ×10⁹/L = cells/µL ÷ 1000. WHO example: improved Neubauer, 4 corner squares (1 mm² each), depth 0.1 mm, 1 in 20 dilution, 188 leukocytes → 9.4 × 10⁹/L.
